title: Ἕκτωρ καὶ ὁ παῖς
about: Hector answers Andromache: he is ashamed to keep out of the fight, and he knows that Troy will fall, but nothing weighs on him as her future does, led off weeping to weave and carry water in Argos; he wishes to be dead before he hears her cry. He reaches for his son, who shrinks from the helmet’s horsehair crest; his parents laugh, he lays the helmet on the ground, kisses the boy and prays that he may become a better man than his father. He puts the child into his wife’s arms, tells her not to grieve beyond what fate allows and to go to her work, since war is men’s business, and puts on his helmet. Andromache goes home looking back, and the women in the house begin to mourn him while he lives. Paris, armoured, runs through the city like a horse let loose, and overtakes Hector with an apology for his delay. Hector answers that no fair man would belittle his fighting, but that he holds back by choice, and the shame of it grieves Hector when he hears the Trojans speak; they set out together.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε μέγας κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ·
sentences.l: Her then in turn addressed great Hector of the glancing helmet:
sentences.i: Then great Hector of the glancing helmet spoke to her in turn:
sentences.n: Hector answers Andromache, whose speech closed the last part. τὴν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε ‘and her in turn he addressed’: προσέειπε is the epic aorist of προσεῖπον ‘address’, and αὖτε ‘in turn’ marks a reply. μέγας κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ ‘great Hector of the glancing helmet’ is his stock epithet, translated every time; κορυθαίολος is κόρυς ‘helmet’ with αἰόλος ‘quick-moving, glancing’.

sentences.t: ἦ καὶ ἐμοὶ τάδε πάντα μέλει γύναι·
sentences.l: “Truly, to me too all this is a care, woman;
sentences.i: “I too care about all this, woman;
sentences.n: He grants that her fear is his own. ἦ καὶ ‘truly, I too’; τάδε πάντα ‘all this’ is what she has just said; μέλει ‘is a care to’ takes the dative ἐμοί. γύναι is the vocative of γυνή, the plain word ‘woman’ in address. The dot closes the admission, and ἀλλά in the next unit turns against it.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ μάλ’ αἰνῶς
αἰδέομαι Τρῶας καὶ Τρῳάδας ἑλκεσιπέπλους,
αἴ κε κακὸς ὣς νόσφιν ἀλυσκάζω πολέμοιο·
sentences.i: but I am terribly ashamed before the Trojans and the Trojan women with their trailing robes, if I should hold aloof from the war, shunning it like a base man;
sentences.n: His first reason for going back to the fight is shame before the city. αἰδέομαι with the accusative is ‘feel shame before’, a respect for others’ opinion. Τρῳάδας ἑλκεσιπέπλους ‘the Trojan women trailing-robed’: ἑλκεσίπεπλος is ἕλκω ‘drag’ with πέπλος ‘robe’, a stock epithet for Trojan women. αἴ κε is the Homeric εἰ κε ‘if’, here with the subjunctive ἀλυσκάζω, ‘if I should shun’; ἀλυσκάζω is a frequentative of ἀλύσκω ‘avoid’. κακὸς ὣς ‘like a base man’, κακός in battle meaning cowardly; νόσφιν ‘apart from’ takes the genitive πολέμοιο.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ με θυμὸς ἄνωγεν, ἐπεὶ μάθον ἔμμεναι ἐσθλὸς
αἰεὶ καὶ πρώτοισι μετὰ Τρώεσσι μάχεσθαι
ἀρνύμενος πατρός τε μέγα κλέος ἠδ’ ἐμὸν αὐτοῦ.
sentences.l:
nor does my heart bid me, since I have learned to be good
always and among the foremost Trojans to fight,
winning my father’s great glory and my own.
sentences.i: nor does my heart bid me do so, since I have learned always to be good and to fight among the foremost Trojans, winning great glory for my father and for myself.
sentences.n: The second reason, which is his whole character. οὐδέ με θυμὸς ἄνωγεν ‘nor does my heart bid me’ leaves the thing refused to be understood from the line before: to hold aloof. μάθον is the aorist of μανθάνω ‘learn’ (unaugmented), and ἐσθλός ‘good’ is the word for a man good in battle, that is brave. πρώτοισι μετὰ Τρώεσσι ‘among the foremost Trojans’; ἀρνύμενος ‘winning’ is a present participle, striving to win. ἐμὸν αὐτοῦ ‘my own’ stands with κλέος ‘glory’, which is both his father’s and his.

sentences.t: εὖ γὰρ ἐγὼ τόδε οἶδα κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν·
sentences.l: for well I know this in mind and in heart:
sentences.i: For I know this well, in my mind and heart:
sentences.n: This line stands in the Iliad before (4.163), and its English is the same here. εὖ γάρ ‘for well’ gives the ground of what he is about to say: he knows it for certain. οἶδα is a perfect with present sense, ‘I know’. κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν ‘in mind and in heart’ is a formula for knowing inwardly. The colon opens the prophecy that follows.

sentences.t:
ἔσσεται ἦμαρ ὅτ’ ἄν ποτ’ ὀλώλῃ Ἴλιος ἱρὴ
καὶ Πρίαμος καὶ λαὸς ἐϋμμελίω Πριάμοιο.
sentences.l:
there will be a day when at some time shall have perished sacred Ilium
and Priam and the people of Priam of the good ash-spear,
sentences.i: There will come a day when sacred Ilium will have perished, and Priam, and the people of Priam of the good ash-spear,
sentences.n: The day of Troy’s fall, stated as certain; these two lines are Agamemnon’s words at 4.164–165, and the English is the same, down to the comma that the Greek here replaces with a full stop. ὅτ’ ἄν ποτ’ is ‘when at some time’, with the subjunctive ὀλώλῃ, the perfect of ὄλλυμι ‘perish’, so the ruin is seen as complete. The subjects are Ἴλιος ἱρή ‘sacred Ilium’, Πρίαμος, and the λαός ‘people’ of Priam, whose stock epithet ἐϋμμελίω is ‘of the good ash-spear’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὔ μοι Τρώων τόσσον μέλει ἄλγος ὀπίσσω,
οὔτ’ αὐτῆς Ἑκάβης οὔτε Πριάμοιο ἄνακτος
οὔτε κασιγνήτων, οἵ κεν πολέες τε καὶ ἐσθλοὶ
ἐν κονίῃσι πέσοιεν ὑπ’ ἀνδράσι δυσμενέεσσιν,
sentences.l:
But not so much does the pain of the Trojans hereafter concern me,
neither of Hecuba herself nor of Priam the king
nor of my brothers, who, many and good,
in the dust may fall beneath ill-disposed men,
sentences.i: But the pain to come for the Trojans does not trouble me so much, nor for Hecuba herself, nor for Priam the king, nor for my brothers, many and good as they are, who may fall in the dust beneath ill-disposed men,
sentences.n: What troubles him most. The sentence is a comparison and is cut at the comma only because it runs to six lines: ἀλλ’ οὔ μοι … τόσσον μέλει ἄλγος ‘but not so much does the pain concern me’ is completed by ὅσσον σεῦ ‘as much as of you’ at the start of the next unit. Τρώων … ὀπίσσω ‘of the Trojans hereafter’ is the pain still to come. The three genitives, αὐτῆς Ἑκάβης, Πριάμοιο ἄνακτος and κασιγνήτων, each follow οὔτε. οἵ κεν … πέσοιεν is an optative with κεν, ‘who might fall’; δυσμενέεσσιν ‘ill-disposed’ is the dative plural of δυσμενής, used here of enemies.

sentences.t:
ὅσσον σεῦ, ὅτε κέν τις Ἀχαιῶν χαλκοχιτώνων
δακρυόεσσαν ἄγηται ἐλεύθερον ἦμαρ ἀπούρας·
sentences.l:
as much as of you, when some one of the bronze-shirted Achaeans
leads you off weeping, the day of freedom having taken away;
sentences.i: as it does for you, when one of the bronze-shirted Achaeans leads you away in tears, taking from you the day of freedom;
sentences.n: This completes the comparison begun in the unit before: it is for Andromache above all that he fears. ὅτε κέν τις … ἄγηται is ‘whenever some one … leads’, the subjunctive with κεν. δακρυόεσσαν ‘weeping’ is the accusative that goes with the unspoken σέ ‘you’. ἐλεύθερον ἦμαρ ‘the day of freedom’ is the free state she will lose, the opposite of the δούλιον ἦμαρ ‘day of slavery’ at 463; ἀπούρας is the aorist participle of ἀπαυράω ‘take away’. Ἀχαιῶν χαλκοχιτώνων ‘of the bronze-shirted Achaeans’ is the stock epithet.

sentences.t:
καί κεν ἐν Ἄργει ἐοῦσα πρὸς ἄλλης ἱστὸν ὑφαίνοις,
καί κεν ὕδωρ φορέοις Μεσσηΐδος ἢ Ὑπερείης
πόλλ’ ἀεκαζομένη, κρατερὴ δ’ ἐπικείσετ’ ἀνάγκη·
sentences.i: And in Argos, at another woman’s bidding, you might weave a web, and carry water from Messeis or Hypereia, much against your will, and strong necessity will lie upon you;
sentences.n: He pictures what captivity will mean. καί κεν … ὑφαίνοις, καί κεν … φορέοις are optatives with κεν, ‘you might weave’, ‘you might carry’. ἐν Ἄργει ἐοῦσα ‘being in Argos’; πρὸς ἄλλης is ‘from the side of another’ woman, that is at her bidding; ἱστόν here is the web being woven. Μεσσηΐδος ἢ Ὑπερείης are the genitives of two names, Messeis and Hypereia, the places the water is fetched from; the text gives no more. πόλλ’ ἀεκαζομένη ‘much against your will’ (ἀεκαζομένη is a participle, ‘unwilling’); ἐπικείσετ’ is the future of ἐπίκειμαι ‘lie upon’, and κρατερή is ‘strong’.

sentences.t: καί ποτέ τις εἴπῃσιν ἰδὼν κατὰ δάκρυ χέουσαν·
sentences.l: And at some time someone may say, seeing you down a tear shedding:
sentences.i: and some day someone may say, seeing you shed tears:
sentences.n: He imagines what will be said of her. εἴπῃσιν is the Homeric subjunctive of εἶπον ‘say’, with the old ending -σιν, and καί ποτέ τις ‘and some day someone’ makes it a possible event. κατὰ δάκρυ χέουσαν ‘shedding tears’ is the formula, with κατά in tmesis, agreeing with the unspoken σέ ‘you’. The colon opens what the onlooker says.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορος ἥδε γυνὴ ὃς ἀριστεύεσκε μάχεσθαι
Τρώων ἱπποδάμων ὅτε Ἴλιον ἀμφεμάχοντο.
sentences.l:
‘Of Hector this is the wife, who used to be the best at fighting
of the horse-taming Trojans, when they fought around Ilium.’
sentences.i: ‘This is the wife of Hector, who used to be the best at fighting among the Trojans, tamers of horses, when they fought around Ilium.’
sentences.n: The onlooker’s words, within Hector’s own speech. Ἕκτορος ἥδε γυνή ‘of Hector this woman, the wife’. ὃς ἀριστεύεσκε μάχεσθαι ‘who used to be the best in fighting’: ἀριστεύεσκε is an imperfect with the iterative suffix -σκ-, ‘was always the best’. Τρώων ἱπποδάμων ‘of the horse-taming Trojans’ is a partitive genitive after ἀριστεύεσκε, ‘best among’; ἱππόδαμοι is the stock epithet of the Trojans. ὅτε … ἀμφεμάχοντο ‘when they fought around’ Ilium, an imperfect with the preposition ἀμφί joined to the verb.

sentences.t: ὥς ποτέ τις ἐρέει·
sentences.l: So at some time someone will say;
sentences.i: So someone will say some day;
sentences.n: This closes the onlooker’s imagined words. ὥς ‘so’ looks back to what he said; ἐρέει is the epic future of ἐρέω ‘will say’ (Attic ἐρεῖ), now stated flatly, and the ano teleia closes it.

sentences.t:
σοὶ δ’ αὖ νέον ἔσσεται ἄλγος
χήτεϊ τοιοῦδ’ ἀνδρὸς ἀμύνειν δούλιον ἦμαρ.
sentences.l:
and for you again a new pain will be
from lack of such a man to ward off the day of slavery.
sentences.i: and for you in turn there will be a fresh pain, for want of such a man to ward off a day of slavery.
sentences.n: The pain he cannot spare her. σοὶ δ’ αὖ ‘and for you in turn’ turns from what others will say to what she will suffer: νέον ἄλγος ‘a new pain’, fresh grief for her because she will have no such husband to ward off slavery. χήτεϊ is a dative of ‘lack, want of’, with the genitive τοιοῦδ’ ἀνδρός ‘such a man’. ἀμύνειν ‘to ward off’ is an infinitive of purpose, and δούλιον ἦμαρ ‘a day of slavery’ is the state of a slave, as νόστιμον ἦμαρ is the state of homecoming.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά με τεθνηῶτα χυτὴ κατὰ γαῖα καλύπτοι
πρίν γέ τι σῆς τε βοῆς σοῦ θ’ ἑλκηθμοῖο πυθέσθαι.
sentences.l:
But me dead may the heaped earth cover
before I learn anything of your outcry and of your being dragged away.”
sentences.i: But may the heaped earth cover me in death before I hear anything of your cries or of your being dragged away.”
sentences.n: He ends with a wish for his own death first. καλύπτοι is an optative of wish, ‘may it cover’, with τεθνηῶτα, the perfect participle of θνῄσκω, ‘dead’, agreeing with με. χυτὴ γαῖα ‘heaped earth’ is the burial mound. πρίν γέ τι … πυθέσθαι ‘before I learn anything’ takes the genitive: σῆς βοῆς ‘of your cry’ and σοῦ ἑλκηθμοῖο ‘of your being dragged away’ (ἑλκηθμός is a rare noun from ἕλκω ‘drag’). His speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν οὗ παιδὸς ὀρέξατο φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ·
sentences.l: So having spoken, for his son reached out glorious Hector;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and glorious Hector reached out for his son;
sentences.n: Narration resumes, and the scene with the child begins. ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ is the usual closing of a speech. οὗ is the possessive ὅς in the genitive, ‘his own’, agreeing with παιδός ‘child, son’, which depends on ὀρέξατο, ‘reached out for’, which takes the genitive. φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ ‘glorious Hector’ is a stock epithet, translated every time.

sentences.t:
ἂψ δ’ ὃ πάϊς πρὸς κόλπον ἐϋζώνοιο τιθήνης
ἐκλίνθη ἰάχων πατρὸς φίλου ὄψιν ἀτυχθεὶς
ταρβήσας χαλκόν τε ἰδὲ λόφον ἱππιοχαίτην,
δεινὸν ἀπ’ ἀκροτάτης κόρυθος νεύοντα νοήσας.
sentences.l:
but back the child to the bosom of the well-girdled nurse
leaned, crying out, at his dear father’s sight dazed with fear,
terrified at the bronze and the horse-maned crest,
dreadfully nodding from the helmet’s topmost point, having noticed it.
sentences.i: But the child shrank back against the bosom of his well-girdled nurse, crying out, dazed with fear at the sight of his dear father, terrified by the bronze and the horse-maned crest, which he saw nodding dreadfully from the top of the helmet.
sentences.n: The baby’s fright. ἂψ … ἐκλίνθη is the aorist passive of κλίνω ‘lean’, here ‘shrank back leaning’; ἰάχων ‘crying out’. ἀτυχθείς is an aorist passive participle of ἀτύζομαι ‘be struck with fear’, with πατρὸς φίλου ὄψιν ‘his dear father’s sight’ as its accusative. ἐϋζώνοιο is ‘well-girdled’, ἐΰ ‘well’ with ζώνη ‘girdle’. ταρβήσας ‘terrified’; χαλκόν ‘the bronze’ is the metal of the helmet; ἱππιοχαίτην ‘horse-maned’ (ἵππος ‘horse’ with χαίτη ‘mane’) describes the λόφος ‘crest’. νεύοντα νοήσας ‘having noticed it nodding’: the participle is of νεύω.

sentences.t: ἐκ δ’ ἐγέλασσε πατήρ τε φίλος καὶ πότνια μήτηρ·
sentences.l: And aloud laughed his dear father and his lady mother;
sentences.i: His dear father and his lady mother laughed aloud;
sentences.n: The parents laugh. ἐκ δ’ ἐγέλασσε is ‘laughed out’, with ἐκ in tmesis (the preposition parted from its verb); the verb is singular though two people laugh, because it agrees with the first subject. πότνια μήτηρ ‘lady mother’ keeps the table’s ‘lady’ for πότνια.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκ’ ἀπὸ κρατὸς κόρυθ’ εἵλετο φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ,
καὶ τὴν μὲν κατέθηκεν ἐπὶ χθονὶ παμφανόωσαν·
sentences.l:
At once from his head the helmet took glorious Hector,
and it he set down upon the ground, all-shining;
sentences.i: At once glorious Hector took the helmet from his head and set it down on the ground, all-shining;
sentences.n: Hector takes off the helmet. ἀπὸ κρατὸς … εἵλετο ‘took from the head’, with ἀπό in tmesis, and κόρυθ’ the elided accusative of κόρυς ‘helmet’. καὶ τὴν μέν ‘and it, for its part’, with κατέθηκεν ‘set down’; παμφανόωσαν ‘all-shining’ is a participle of παμφανάω agreeing with τήν.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ ὃν φίλον υἱὸν ἐπεὶ κύσε πῆλέ τε χερσὶν
εἶπε δ’ ἐπευξάμενος Διί τ’ ἄλλοισίν τε θεοῖσι·
sentences.l:
But he, when his own dear son he had kissed and dandled in his hands,
spoke, praying, to Zeus and the other gods:
sentences.i: And when he had kissed his own dear son and dandled him in his hands, he prayed to Zeus and the other gods, saying:
sentences.n: He kisses the child and prays. αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ ‘but he’; ὃν φίλον υἱόν is ‘his own dear son’, because ὅς here is the possessive, not the relative. πῆλε is an unaugmented aorist of πάλλω ‘swing, toss’, so ‘dandled’. εἶπε δ’ ἐπευξάμενος ‘spoke, praying’: ἐπευξάμενος is the aorist participle of ἐπεύχομαι. Διί τ’ ἄλλοισίν τε θεοῖσι ‘to Zeus and to the other gods’. The colon opens his prayer.

sentences.t:
Ζεῦ ἄλλοι τε θεοὶ δότε δὴ καὶ τόνδε γενέσθαι
παῖδ’ ἐμὸν ὡς καὶ ἐγώ περ ἀριπρεπέα Τρώεσσιν,
ὧδε βίην τ’ ἀγαθόν, καὶ Ἰλίου ἶφι ἀνάσσειν·
sentences.i: “Zeus and you other gods, grant that this son of mine too may become, as I am, outstanding among the Trojans, so good in strength, and may rule Ilium powerfully;
sentences.n: The prayer for his son. Ζεῦ ἄλλοι τε θεοί ‘Zeus and you other gods’ is a vocative; δότε is the aorist imperative of δίδωμι, and δότε … γενέσθαι ‘grant that he become’ takes an accusative and infinitive, with καὶ τόνδε … παῖδ’ ἐμόν ‘this child of mine too’. ὡς καὶ ἐγώ περ ‘even as I too’. ἀριπρεπέα ‘outstanding’ is the stock word for a man who stands out. ὧδε βίην τ’ ἀγαθόν ‘so good in strength’, with βίην an accusative of respect. καὶ Ἰλίου ἶφι ἀνάσσειν ‘and to be lord over Ilium with force’, ἀνάσσω taking the genitive.

sentences.t:
καί ποτέ τις εἴποι πατρός γ’ ὅδε πολλὸν ἀμείνων
ἐκ πολέμου ἀνιόντα·
sentences.l:
and some day may someone say, ‘This one is far better than his father,’
as he comes back from the war;
sentences.i: and some day may someone say, ‘This one is far better than his father,’ as he comes back from war;
sentences.n: He prays that the boy outdo him. καί ποτέ τις εἴποι ‘and some day may someone say’ is an optative of wish. The words said are πατρός γ’ ὅδε πολλὸν ἀμείνων ‘this one is far better than his father’, with the comparative ἀμείνων ‘better’ and the genitive of comparison πατρός; ἐκ πολέμου ἀνιόντα ‘as he comes back from war’ is outside the quotation and describes the boy, with the participle in the accusative.

sentences.t:
φέροι δ’ ἔναρα βροτόεντα
κτείνας δήϊον ἄνδρα, χαρείη δὲ φρένα μήτηρ.
sentences.l:
and may he carry bloody spoils,
having killed a hostile man, and may his mother rejoice in her mind.”
sentences.i: and may he carry the bloody spoils of a hostile man he has killed, and may his mother be glad in her mind.”
sentences.n: The prayer’s last wishes; both verbs are optatives of wish. ἔναρα βροτόεντα are ‘bloody spoils’, the armour stripped from a slain enemy (βροτόεις, ‘bloody’, is from βρότος ‘gore’). κτείνας δήϊον ἄνδρα ‘having killed a hostile man’. χαρείη is the aorist optative passive of χαίρω, and φρένα is an accusative of respect, ‘in her mind’. His prayer ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν ἀλόχοιο φίλης ἐν χερσὶν ἔθηκε
παῖδ’ ἑόν·
sentences.l:
So having spoken, in his dear wife’s hands he placed
his own child;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and placed his own son in the hands of his dear wife;
sentences.n: He gives the child back. ὣς εἰπών is the usual end of a speech. ἀλόχοιο φίλης ‘of his dear wife’ is an epic genitive in -οιο, with ἐν χερσὶν ἔθηκε ‘placed in her hands’. ἑόν is the possessive ‘his own’, in agreement with παῖδ’.

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ ἄρα μιν κηώδεϊ δέξατο κόλπῳ
δακρυόεν γελάσασα·
sentences.l:
and she received him in her fragrant bosom,
laughing tearfully;
sentences.i: and she took him to her fragrant bosom, laughing through her tears;
sentences.n: Andromache takes the child. ἣ δ’ ἄρα ‘and she then’; δέξατο is the aorist of δέχομαι ‘receive’ and μιν ‘him’ is the child. κηώδεϊ ‘fragrant’ is the epic dative of κηώδης, a word for a sweet smell. δακρυόεν γελάσασα ‘laughing tearfully’: δακρυόεν is a neuter accusative used as an adverb, ‘tearfully’, and the participle is of γελάω.

sentences.t:
πόσις δ’ ἐλέησε νοήσας,
χειρί τέ μιν κατέρεξεν ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε·
sentences.l:
and her husband pitied her, having noticed,
and stroked her with his hand, and spoke a word, and called her by name:
sentences.i: and her husband pitied her as he looked at her, and stroked her with his hand, and spoke, calling her by name:
sentences.n: Hector’s tenderness. πόσις is ‘husband’. ἐλέησε is the aorist of ἐλεέω ‘pity’, and νοήσας ‘having noticed’ takes the thing seen to be her tearful face, which the Greek leaves unspoken. The second line is a formula of gentle address: χειρί τέ μιν κατέρεξεν ‘and stroked her with his hand’ (μιν is ‘her’ here), ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε ‘and spoke a word and called her by name’, with ἔκ in tmesis with ὀνόμαζε. The colon opens his speech.

sentences.t: δαιμονίη μή μοί τι λίην ἀκαχίζεο θυμῷ·
sentences.l: “Strange woman, for me not at all too much be distressed in heart;
sentences.i: “Strange woman, do not grieve over me too much in your heart;
sentences.n: He begins to comfort her. δαιμονίη is the feminine vocative of δαιμόνιος, ‘strange one’; it is a form of address whose force is not certain (gentle or reproving), and ‘strange woman’ keeps the word without choosing. μή … ἀκαχίζεο is a prohibition, the present imperative middle of ἀκαχίζω ‘distress’, ‘do not be distressed’. μοί ‘for me’; τι λίην ‘at all too much’.

sentences.t: οὐ γάρ τίς μ’ ὑπὲρ αἶσαν ἀνὴρ Ἄϊδι προϊάψει·
sentences.l: for not any man me beyond due measure to Hades will send forth;
sentences.i: for no man will fling me down to Hades beyond my due measure;
sentences.n: His reason: his death is not in any man’s gift. οὐ γάρ τίς μ’ … ἀνήρ ‘for no man … me’. ὑπὲρ αἶσαν ‘beyond due measure’ is set against κατ’ αἶσαν ‘according to due measure’: αἶσα is the share allotted to each man. Ἄϊδι is the dative of Ἄϊς, a by-form of Ἅιδης ‘Hades’, and προϊάψει is the future of προϊάπτω ‘send forth’, the verb used at 1.3 of souls sent to Hades.

sentences.t:
μοῖραν δ’ οὔ τινά φημι πεφυγμένον ἔμμεναι ἀνδρῶν,
οὐ κακὸν οὐδὲ μὲν ἐσθλόν, ἐπὴν τὰ πρῶτα γένηται.
sentences.l:
and fate, no one, I say, has escaped, of men,
neither the base nor indeed the good, when first he is born.
sentences.i: and I say that no man has escaped his fate, neither the base nor the good, once he has been born.
sentences.n: The rule behind it. μοῖραν … οὔ τινά φημι πεφυγμένον ἔμμεναι ἀνδρῶν ‘I say that none of men has escaped fate’: φημί with an accusative and infinitive, and πεφυγμένον ἔμμεναι is the perfect of φεύγω ‘have escaped’. οὐ κακὸν οὐδὲ μὲν ἐσθλόν ‘neither the base nor indeed the good’, κακός and ἐσθλός being ‘base’ and ‘good’, the coward and the brave man. ἐπὴν τὰ πρῶτα γένηται ‘once first he is born’, a subjunctive with ἐπήν (= ἐπεὶ ἄν).

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ εἰς οἶκον ἰοῦσα τὰ σ’ αὐτῆς ἔργα κόμιζε
ἱστόν τ’ ἠλακάτην τε, καὶ ἀμφιπόλοισι κέλευε
ἔργον ἐποίχεσθαι·
sentences.i: Go instead into the house and attend to your own work, the loom and the distaff, and tell your handmaids to get on with their tasks;
sentences.n: He sends her home to her work. This is the same passage, in the same English, as Odyssey 1.356–358 (Telemachus to Penelope); the Greek here has no comma after κόμιζε. εἰς οἶκον ἰοῦσα ‘going into the house’, τὰ σ’ αὐτῆς ἔργα ‘your own tasks’, with κόμιζε an imperative, ‘look after’. ἱστόν is the loom, ἠλακάτη the distaff; ἀμφιπόλοισι ‘to the handmaids’ takes κέλευε ‘give orders’ and the infinitive ἐποίχεσθαι ‘to ply’.

sentences.t:
πόλεμος δ’ ἄνδρεσσι μελήσει
πᾶσι, μάλιστα δ’ ἐμοί, τοὶ Ἰλίῳ ἐγγεγάασιν.
sentences.l:
and war will be the care of men,
of all, and most of all of me, of those who in Ilium were born.”
sentences.i: and war will be the concern of all the men who were born in Ilium, and of me most of all.”
sentences.n: The reason she should go: war is men’s work. πόλεμος δ’ ἄνδρεσσι μελήσει ‘and war will be a care to men’, with the dative ἄνδρεσσι (epic -εσσι) and the future of μέλω. πᾶσι, μάλιστα δ’ ἐμοί ‘to all, and most of all to me’; τοί is the relative ‘who’, here with a plural antecedent, and ἐγγεγάασιν is the epic perfect of ἐγγίγνομαι ‘have been born in’. His speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας κόρυθ’ εἵλετο φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ
ἵππουριν·
sentences.l:
So then having spoken, his helmet took glorious Hector,
the horse-tailed one;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and glorious Hector took up his helmet with its horsetail plume;
sentences.n: Hector puts the helmet on again. ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας ‘so then having spoken’ closes the speech. εἵλετο ‘took up’, with κόρυθ’ ‘helmet’ and the adjective ἵππουριν ‘horse-tailed’, which waits at the start of the next line; ἵππουρις describes the crest. φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ ‘glorious Hector’ is the stock epithet.

sentences.t:
ἄλοχος δὲ φίλη οἶκον δὲ βεβήκει
ἐντροπαλιζομένη, θαλερὸν κατὰ δάκρυ χέουσα.
sentences.l:
but his dear wife to the house had gone,
turning back again and again, an abundant tear down shedding.
sentences.i: and his dear wife went home, turning back again and again, shedding abundant tears.
sentences.n: Andromache goes home. ἄλοχος δὲ φίλη ‘but his dear wife’; οἶκον δέ is ‘to the house’, with the ending -δε of motion towards. βεβήκει is the pluperfect of βαίνω, ‘had set off, was on her way’. ἐντροπαλιζομένη is a participle of a rare frequentative, built on ἐν and the root of τρέπω ‘turn’, and describes her turning round repeatedly to look back. θαλερὸν κατὰ δάκρυ χέουσα ‘shedding an abundant tear’ (θαλερόν is ‘abundant’).

sentences.t:
αἶψα δ’ ἔπειθ’ ἵκανε δόμους εὖ ναιετάοντας
Ἕκτορος ἀνδροφόνοιο, κιχήσατο δ’ ἔνδοθι πολλὰς
ἀμφιπόλους, τῇσιν δὲ γόον πάσῃσιν ἐνῶρσεν.
sentences.l:
And quickly then she came to the well-inhabited house
of man-slaying Hector, and found within many
handmaids, among all of whom she roused lament.
sentences.i: She quickly came to the well-inhabited house of man-slaying Hector, and found many handmaids inside, and roused a lament among them all.
sentences.n: She reaches home; the first line also stands at 6.370, where it is Hector who arrives. αἶψα δ’ ἔπειτ’ ἵκανε ‘and quickly then she came’, the subject being Andromache. δόμους εὖ ναιετάοντας ‘the well-inhabited house’, with a plural noun for a single house. Ἕκτορος ἀνδροφόνοιο ‘of man-slaying Hector’ is the stock epithet, ἀνδροφόνος being ἀνήρ with the root of φόνος. κιχήσατο ‘found’; ἀμφιπόλους are her women servants. τῇσιν δὲ γόον πάσῃσιν ἐνῶρσεν ‘and among them all she roused lament’: ἐνῶρσεν is the aorist of ἐνόρνυμι.

sentences.t: αἳ μὲν ἔτι ζωὸν γόον Ἕκτορα ᾧ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ·
sentences.l: They then still living lamented Hector in his own house;
sentences.i: So they lamented Hector in his own house while he was still alive;
sentences.n: The women mourn a man who is not dead. αἳ μὲν … γόον is the third-person plural imperfect of γοάω ‘lament’, with Ἕκτορα as the person mourned and ζωὸν ‘living’ agreeing with it. ᾧ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ ‘in his own house’: ᾧ is the possessive, not the relative.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ μιν ἔτ’ ἔφαντο ὑπότροπον ἐκ πολέμοιο
ἵξεσθαι προφυγόντα μένος καὶ χεῖρας Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l:
for not any more did they say that he from the war returning
would come, having escaped the might and the hands of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: for they no longer supposed that he would come back from the fighting, having escaped the might and the hands of the Achaeans.
sentences.n: Why they mourn already. οὐ γάρ μιν ἔτ’ ἔφαντο ‘for they no longer said of him’, ἔφαντο being the imperfect of φημί, ‘they supposed’. ὑπότροπον ‘returning’ and ἵξεσθαι, the future infinitive of ἱκνέομαι ‘come’, go together; προφυγόντα is an aorist participle of προφεύγω ‘escape’. μένος καὶ χεῖρας Ἀχαιῶν ‘the might and the hands of the Achaeans’.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ Πάρις δήθυνεν ἐν ὑψηλοῖσι δόμοισιν,
ἀλλ’ ὅ γ’, ἐπεὶ κατέδυ κλυτὰ τεύχεα ποικίλα χαλκῷ,
σεύατ’ ἔπειτ’ ἀνὰ ἄστυ ποσὶ κραιπνοῖσι πεποιθώς.
sentences.l:
Nor did Paris linger in his high halls,
but he, when he had put on his famous armour, intricate with bronze,
rushed then up through the city, trusting in his rushing feet.
sentences.i: Paris did not linger in his high halls either, but, when he had put on his famous armour, intricate with bronze, he rushed then through the city, trusting in his rushing feet.
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and Paris. οὐδὲ … δήθυνεν ‘nor did he linger’, the aorist of δηθύνω ‘delay’. ἀλλ’ ὅ γ’ ‘but he’; ἐπεὶ κατέδυ … τεύχεα ‘when he put on the armour’, κατέδυ being the aorist of καταδύω. κλυτὰ τεύχεα ποικίλα χαλκῷ ‘famous armour, intricate with bronze’, with the dative χαλκῷ saying what makes it intricate. σεύατ’ is the aorist middle of σεύω ‘rush’; ποσὶ κραιπνοῖσι πεποιθώς ‘trusting in his rushing feet’ takes the dative after the perfect participle of πείθομαι.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτε τις στατὸς ἵππος ἀκοστήσας ἐπὶ φάτνῃ
δεσμὸν ἀπορρήξας θείῃ πεδίοιο κροαίνων
εἰωθὼς λούεσθαι ἐϋρρεῖος ποταμοῖο
κυδιόων·
sentences.l:
And as when some stalled horse, fed on barley at the manger,
having broken the tether, may run over the plain, pounding,
accustomed to bathe in the fair-flowing river,
glorying;
sentences.i: As when some stalled horse, fed on barley at the manger, breaks his tether and runs pounding over the plain, accustomed to bathe in the fair-flowing river, glorying;
sentences.n: A simile for Paris. ὡς δ’ ὅτε ‘as when’ opens it, with the subjunctive θείῃ (of θέω ‘run’) for a general case. στατὸς ἵππος is a horse kept standing in the stall; ἀκοστήσας ἐπὶ φάτνῃ is a rare verb, built on ἀκοστή ‘barley’, ‘fed on barley at the manger’. δεσμὸν ἀπορρήξας ‘having broken the tether’; πεδίοιο is a genitive of the ground covered, and κροαίνων ‘pounding’ describes the hooves. εἰωθὼς λούεσθαι ‘accustomed to bathe’; ἐϋρρεῖος is the genitive of ἐϋρρεής ‘fair-flowing’, and goes with ποταμοῖο. κυδιόων ‘glorying’.

sentences.t:
ὑψοῦ δὲ κάρη ἔχει, ἀμφὶ δὲ χαῖται
ὤμοις ἀΐσσονται·
sentences.l:
and high he holds his head, and about
his shoulders the mane streams;
sentences.i: he holds his head high, and his mane streams about his shoulders;
sentences.n: The horse as he runs. ὑψοῦ δὲ κάρη ἔχει ‘and he holds his head high’; ἀμφὶ δὲ … ὤμοις ‘and about his shoulders’, the dative after ἀμφί. χαῖται is the plural of χαίτη ‘mane’, and ἀΐσσονται is ‘dart, stream’, a present middle in the plural to agree with it.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἀγλαΐηφι πεποιθὼς
ῥίμφά ἑ γοῦνα φέρει μετά τ’ ἤθεα καὶ νομὸν ἵππων·
sentences.l:
and he, trusting in his splendour,
lightly his knees carry him to the haunts and pasture of the horses;
sentences.i: and, trusting in his beauty, his knees carry him lightly to the haunts and pasture of the horses;
sentences.n: The simile’s end. ὃ δ’ ‘and he’, the horse; ἀγλαΐηφι is the instrumental in -φι, ‘in his splendour’, after the participle πεποιθώς ‘trusting’. ῥίμφα ‘lightly’ is an adverb; ἑ ‘him’ is the object of φέρει ‘carries’ and γοῦνα is the epic plural of γόνυ ‘knee’. μετά τ’ ἤθεα καὶ νομὸν ἵππων ‘to the haunts and pasture of the horses’, μετά with the accusative of motion towards.

sentences.t:
ὣς υἱὸς Πριάμοιο Πάρις κατὰ Περγάμου ἄκρης
τεύχεσι παμφαίνων ὥς τ’ ἠλέκτωρ ἐβεβήκει
καγχαλόων, ταχέες δὲ πόδες φέρον·
sentences.i: So Paris, the son of Priam, set out down from high Pergamus, all-shining in his armour like the sun, exulting, and his swift feet bore him;
sentences.n: The simile applied. ὣς … Πάρις ‘so Paris’ answers ὡς δ’ ὅτε; κατὰ Περγάμου ἄκρης ‘down from the high Pergamus’, the citadel of Troy. τεύχεσι παμφαίνων ‘all-shining in his armour’. ὥς τ’ ἠλέκτωρ ‘like the ἠλέκτωρ’: the word is rare, and the usual explanation, followed here, is ‘the sun’, but that is not certain. ἐβεβήκει is the pluperfect of βαίνω, ‘had set out’; καγχαλόων ‘exulting’; ταχέες … πόδες ‘swift feet’.

sentences.t:
αἶψα δ’ ἔπειτα
Ἕκτορα δῖον ἔτετμεν ἀδελφεὸν εὖτ’ ἄρ’ ἔμελλε
στρέψεσθ’ ἐκ χώρης ὅθι ᾗ ὀάριζε γυναικί.
sentences.l:
and quickly then
heavenly Hector his brother he found, just when he was about
to turn away from the place where he was conversing with his own wife.
sentences.i: and soon he came upon his brother, heavenly Hector, just as Hector was about to turn away from the place where he had been talking with his wife.
sentences.n: Paris catches up with Hector. ἔτετμεν is ‘found, came upon’, an aorist with no present in use in Homer. Ἕκτορα δῖον ἀδελφεόν ‘Hector, his heavenly brother’ (δῖος ‘heavenly’ is his stock epithet; ἀδελφεόν is the epic form of ἀδελφόν). εὖτ’ ἄρ’ ἔμελλε ‘just when he was about’, μέλλω taking the future infinitive στρέψεσθαι ‘to turn’. ὅθι ᾗ ὀάριζε γυναικί ‘where he was talking with his own wife’: ᾗ is the possessive, and ὀαρίζω is the verb of intimate talk between husband and wife.

sentences.t: τὸν πρότερος προσέειπεν Ἀλέξανδρος θεοειδής·
sentences.l: Him first addressed Alexander godlike-in-form:
sentences.i: Alexander, godlike in form, spoke to him first:
sentences.n: Paris speaks first. τὸν πρότερος προσέειπεν ‘him first he addressed’, πρότερος ‘first’ agreeing with the speaker; προσέειπεν is the epic aorist of προσεῖπον. Ἀλέξανδρος is Paris’ other name, and θεοειδής ‘godlike in form’ is his stock epithet, translated every time.

sentences.t:
ἠθεῖ’ ἦ μάλα δή σε καὶ ἐσσύμενον κατερύκω
δηθύνων, οὐδ’ ἦλθον ἐναίσιμον ὡς ἐκέλευες;
sentences.l:
“Honoured one, surely indeed I am holding you back, even as you hasten,
by delaying, and did not come in the fitting way, as you bade?”
sentences.i: “My honoured one, am I indeed holding you back, hurrying as you are, by my delay, and did I fail to come as was fitting, as you bade me?”
sentences.n: Paris apologises, as a question. ἠθεῖ’ is the elided vocative of ἠθεῖος, a word of address whose sense is not known; ‘honoured one’ is the guess made for the same word at Odyssey 14.147, and it is the same guess here. ἦ μάλα δή is ‘surely indeed’, introducing the question. ἐσσύμενον ‘hastening’ is the participle of σεύομαι, agreeing with σε; κατερύκω ‘I hold back’, δηθύνων ‘by delaying’. οὐδ’ ἦλθον ‘and did not come’ is still inside the question; ἐναίσιμον ‘in a fitting way’ is a neuter adjective used as an adverb; ὡς ἐκέλευες ‘as you bade’.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed Hector of the glancing helmet:
sentences.i: In answer Hector of the glancing helmet said to him:
sentences.n: Hector replies. τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη ‘and answering him he addressed’, a formula for reply; προσέφη is the aorist of πρόσφημι ‘speak to’. κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ ‘Hector of the glancing helmet’ is the stock epithet, translated every time.

sentences.t:
δαιμόνι’ οὐκ ἄν τίς τοι ἀνὴρ ὃς ἐναίσιμος εἴη
ἔργον ἀτιμήσειε μάχης, ἐπεὶ ἄλκιμός ἐσσι·
sentences.l:
“Strange man, not any man who is one with a sense of what is fitting
would dishonour your work of battle, since you are valiant;
sentences.i: “Strange man, no man with a sense of what is fitting would dishonour your work in battle, since you are valiant;
sentences.n: His answer starts with praise. δαιμόνι’ is the elided vocative of δαιμόνιος ‘strange man’, an address whose force is not certain, gentle here though it leads to a reproach. οὐκ ἄν τίς … ἀτιμήσειε ‘no one would dishonour’ is the optative with ἄν, and τοι is the dative ‘to you’, ‘in your case’. ὃς ἐναίσιμος εἴη ‘who has a sense of what is fitting’ (ἐναίσιμος ‘fitting’); ἀτιμήσειε is the aorist optative of ἀτιμάω (Attic ἀτιμάζω); ἔργον μάχης is ‘the work of battle’. ἐπεὶ ἄλκιμός ἐσσι ‘since you are valiant’.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ ἑκὼν μεθιεῖς τε καὶ οὐκ ἐθέλεις·
sentences.l: but willingly you slacken, and you are unwilling;
sentences.i: but you slack off willingly, and you are unwilling;
sentences.n: Then the reproach. ἑκών ‘willingly’ and μεθιεῖς ‘you slacken’, the Homeric second person of μεθίημι (used without its usual genitive, so simply ‘you slack off’); καὶ οὐκ ἐθέλεις ‘and you are not willing’. The ano teleia stops the sentence before the next, which says what it costs him.

sentences.t:
τὸ δ’ ἐμὸν κῆρ
ἄχνυται ἐν θυμῷ, ὅθ’ ὑπὲρ σέθεν αἴσχε’ ἀκούω
πρὸς Τρώων, οἳ ἔχουσι πολὺν πόνον εἵνεκα σεῖο.
sentences.l:
and my heart
grieves in my spirit, when I hear shameful things about you
from the Trojans, who have much toil on account of you.
sentences.i: and my heart grieves in my spirit, when I hear shameful things said of you by the Trojans, who bear much toil on your account.
sentences.n: What the Trojans say. τὸ δ’ ἐμὸν κῆρ ‘and my heart’ is the subject of ἄχνυται ‘grieves’, with ἐν θυμῷ ‘in my spirit’; the literal layer keeps κῆρ ‘heart’ apart from θυμός ‘spirit’ where they stand together. ὅθ’ ὑπὲρ σέθεν αἴσχε’ ἀκούω ‘when I hear shameful things on your behalf’, σέθεν being the epic genitive of σύ; αἴσχεα is a neuter plural, ‘words of shame’. πρὸς Τρώων ‘from the Trojans’; οἳ ἔχουσι πολὺν πόνον εἵνεκα σεῖο ‘who have much toil for your sake’, with εἵνεκα the epic form of ἕνεκα.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἴομεν·
sentences.l: But let us go;
sentences.i: But come, let us go;
sentences.n: He ends the exchange. ἀλλ’ ἴομεν ‘but let us go’: ἴομεν is the subjunctive of εἶμι ‘go’ in an exhortation, with the short vowel and the plural ending ‘let us’.

sentences.t:
τὰ δ’ ὄπισθεν ἀρεσσόμεθ’, αἴ κέ ποθι Ζεὺς
δώῃ ἐπουρανίοισι θεοῖς αἰειγενέτῃσι
κρητῆρα στήσασθαι ἐλεύθερον ἐν μεγάροισιν
ἐκ Τροίης ἐλάσαντας ἐϋκνήμιδας Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.l:
the rest hereafter we shall put right, if perhaps Zeus
shall grant to the gods of heaven, the forever-born,
to set up a mixing-bowl of freedom in the halls,
having driven out of Troy the well-greaved Achaeans.”
sentences.i: Afterwards we shall put right what is amiss, if Zeus grants that we set up a mixing-bowl of freedom in our halls for the everlasting gods of heaven, once we have driven the well-greaved Achaeans out of Troy.”
sentences.n: The hope with which he ends. τὰ δ’ ὄπισθεν ἀρεσσόμεθ’ ‘the rest hereafter we shall put right’, ἀρεσσόμεθα being the future of ἀρέσκω ‘put right’ and the reproaches the thing mended. αἴ κέ ποθι … δώῃ ‘if perhaps he grants’ is a conditional with the subjunctive. ἐπουρανίοισι θεοῖς αἰειγενέτῃσι ‘the gods of heaven, the forever-born’, a pair of epithets. κρητῆρα … ἐλεύθερον is a mixing-bowl of freedom, set up in thanks to the gods once the Trojans are free; στήσασθαι ‘set up for oneself’, taking the dative θεοῖς ‘for the gods’. ἐλάσαντας is an accusative plural, agreeing with the unspoken ‘us’, ‘having driven’; ἐϋκνήμιδας Ἀχαιούς ‘the well-greaved Achaeans’ is the stock epithet. His speech ends here.
